title.en: Mass-spring cloth and its solver contract

summary: Treat cloth as a solver with declared parameters: what is integrated, at what step, and what makes it explode.
objective: Build a cloth patch whose spring structure, timestep and substep count are visible controls, with an explicit stability report.
intent_signals: Build a cloth simulation whose parameters I can see and change.
Show what happens to cloth when the timestep is too large.
example_prompts: Build a mass-spring cloth patch with visible spring families and a stability readout.
Show cloth pinned at two corners settling under gravity with a declared substep count.
negative_signals: Not a validated textile model: no fabric identification, drape prediction or material testing.
Not a claim of physical accuracy; the parameters are numerical, not measured.
not_for: Not a validated textile model: no fabric identification, drape prediction or material testing.
Not a claim of physical accuracy; the parameters are numerical, not measured.

entities.name: Particle lattice
entities.guidance: Build the cloth as an explicit particle grid with mass per particle, so the simulated object and the rendered mesh are clearly the same thing.

entities.name: Spring families
entities.guidance: Separate structural, shear and bending connections as toggleable families, since removing one produces a visibly different failure.

entities.name: Solver panel
entities.guidance: Show timestep, substeps, damping and the current maximum spring stretch, so instability can be predicted rather than discovered.

state_contract.model: Particle positions and velocities on a fixed lattice with fixed rendered-mesh connectivity, three toggleable spring families (structural, shear, bending) forming the enabled force graph, gravity, velocity damping and pinned particles as hard constraints. Integration is semi-implicit Euler on a fixed step with a declared substep count: each substep accumulates spring forces from rest-length deviation, updates velocity, then updates position from the new velocity. A spring at zero length contributes no direction and is skipped for that substep. Pinning zeroes a particle velocity and releasing it resumes from zero velocity at its current position.
state_contract.authority: The particle state is authoritative; the rendered surface is generated from it every step. A cloth that looks settled while particle velocities are still large is a display error.
actions: Toggle a spring family and observe the failure mode.
Reset particles to the rest configuration.

invariants: Pinned particles never move, regardless of stiffness or timestep.

Particle count and rendered-mesh connectivity stay constant during a run; toggling a spring family changes only the enabled force graph, and the scene marks the run as restarted so results before and after are not compared as one experiment.
The stability report is derived from measured stretch or velocity, not from a fixed assumption that the settings are safe.
motion_guidance: Advance the solver on a fixed step with accumulated remainder and interpolate rendering, so visual smoothness never hides step size.
Let the viewer single-step the solver; an exploding cloth is most informative one step at a time.
known_limits: Explicit integration of stiff springs is fragile: a stiffness that works at one timestep can diverge at another.
Self-collision and cloth-to-body contact are separate problems that this recipe does not solve.

Stretch and velocity thresholds flag a diverging run; they do not certify stability, and the cited engine documentation supports generic timestep and integrator cautions rather than a stability guarantee for this particular spring network.
Authored guidance only: no scene runtime, rendering or numerical calibration has been run for this recipe.

claims.statement: Physics engine documentation states that the simulation timestep must be chosen carefully: too large and the simulation becomes unstable, too small and computation is wasted, and integrating velocity-dependent forces implicitly can be markedly more stable than an explicit single-step method.
claims.scope: Documented behaviour of one engine and version, cited here to justify exposing timestep and integrator choice rather than to certify any particular cloth solver.

object_craft.structure: A visible grid of particle markers in debug view with the rendered cloth surface generated from the same positions.
object_craft.material: Debug markers use a reserved accent that is off by default; the cloth surface uses a two-sided material so the back face is not black.
object_craft.articulation: Every visual vertex follows its particle; no smoothing may move a vertex away from its particle position.

object_craft.structure: Line sets drawn per family with distinct dash patterns so overlapping families remain separable.
object_craft.material: Three neutral values rather than three hues, so the debug view stays readable over the cloth.
object_craft.articulation: Spring overlays are rebuilt from current particle positions every frame, so an enabled family always draws between the particles it actually acts on even though connectivity is unchanged.

physical_contract.scope: Mass-spring integration with gravity, damping and pin constraints; no self-collision, aerodynamics or material calibration.
driving: Spring forces from rest-length deviation, gravity and velocity damping.
contact: No contact is modelled: cloth-to-body and cloth-to-cloth collision are out of scope for this recipe, and the solver contract makes no provision for them.
physical_contract.timestep: Fixed step with a stated substep count and accumulated remainder, integrated semi-implicitly; rendering interpolates between completed steps.
checks: Pinned particles stay exactly fixed for the whole run.
Reducing the timestep removes the divergence seen at a larger one, or the report says it did not.
